reconcile.connective: Clarke attributes Mary's failure to recognize Jesus to her grief and utter unpreparedness for a resurrection she had not yet conceived possible.

discrepancy.connective: Ehrman argues Matthew, Luke, and John give genuinely irreconcilable accounts of who saw the risen Jesus, not stages of one harmonized scene.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, Jesus, Interrupted (HarperOne, 2009), pp. 47-55

excerpts.excerpt_text: Mary was so absorbed in grief that she paid but little attention to the person of our Lord, and therefore did not at first discern it to be him; nor could she imagine such an appearance possible, as she had no conception of his resurrection from the dead. She was therefore every way unprepared to recognize the person of our Lord.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly explains why Mary failed to recognize Jesus in John's account despite Matthew's women recognizing him instantly — grief and lack of resurrection-expectation, not a genuine narrative conflict.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley's 'Christ's resurrection — certain narratives; different account of it' section (pp. 327-330) treats Matt. 28:1-10, Mark 16:1-14, Luke 24:1-12, and John 20:1-18 together, arguing the accounts fit into one sequence: Mary Magdalene leaves the other women early to fetch Peter and John, the remaining women meet the angels and then Jesus on the road (Matthew), and Mary Magdalene, having returned to the tomb a second time alone, meets Jesus separately and does not at first know him (John).
